newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China rubber tappers struggle back after typhoons.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China rubber tappers struggle back after typhoons.

text.p: When Typhoon Willie roared across China's tropical Hainan province last September it did more than shred the upper branches of the island's stately rubber trees and shatter hopes for a bumper harvest.
The storm also sapped the enthusiasm of tappers already weary of hard labour and the uncertain returns decreed by international rubber prices, farmers and officials say.
But the provincial government is optimistic that output will bounce back this year, said Xing Yiqiao of the Hainan Provincial Agricultural Department.

"You can see how the tops of all our rubber trees have been blown down," said Liang Senkui, vice director of a state farm in southern Hainan, gazing morosely at the damage left by Typhoon Willie and by Typhoon Niki, which scoured the island in August.

"The 1996 typhoons caused 17 million yuan ($2.0 million) in losses at this farm," said Liang, whose Xinglong Overseas Chinese Farm is one of about 90 government-run agricultural enterprises that are the backbone of Hainan rubber production.
Typhoons killed at least 45 people, left hundreds homeless and cut Hainan's rubber output to around 230,000 tonnes in 1996, down from 260,000 tonnes the year before, officials said.
This year, the island hoped to push production back to 1995 levels, said agricultural official Xing.
"By 2000 we want to reach 350,000 tonnes a year," Xing said in an interview, adding that rubber production was a vital part of the Hainan economy.
The tropical island's tappers and processors produced two thirds of China's total rubber output and earned around 3.0 billion yuan in 1995 -- a quarter of Hainan's income from agriculture, he said.
SEEDS OF SUCCESS BROUGHT FROM AFAR
Hainan's rubber industry began in the early years of this century, when former emigrants to Southeast Asia began returning to their ancestral homeland with new skills.
"In 1906, our Overseas Chinese first brought rubber tree seeds and planted them in Hainan," said Xing.
Development was slow at first, with annual production of just 200 tonnes by the time the conquering armies of China's Communist Party took control of the island in 1950, he said.

But demand and production soared as Beijing launched a nationwide programme of socialist industrialisation and a new wave of thousands of returned Overseas Chinese hacked out plantations from Hainan's malarial wastes.

Rubber now accounted for more than 368,000 hectares (909,300 acres) of the 440,200 hectares (1.08 million acres) of tropical crops planted in Hainan, Xing said. "Rubber is the base of the economy in our villages," he said.
Large state farms, a remnant of efforts to modernise agriculture through collectivisation, still dominate Hainan rubber production, although workers tap and tend the trees on a contract basis.

Residents of the sprawling Xinglong Overseas Chinese Farm, carved out by returned emigrants in the 1950s, said the toil involved made it a poor alternative to more lucrative opportunities in the area's burgeoning tourist trade.
To make the most of their trees, tappers had to labour in the earliest hours of the morning and were tormented by the insects that ruled the plantations before dawn, they said.
Motivating farm workers was a vital issue, said farm vice director Liang, an ethnic Chinese who was born in Indonesia but returned to his homeland in 1960.
"It's very important to boost the workers' enthusiasm," he said in an interview.
PRICES FLUCTUATE, ASSETS AGEING

Xing said farmers benefited hugely when central planners liberated rubber prices in the early 1990s, but saw the value of the white sap that trickled from their towering trees erode when international prices later slipped.
Agricultural officials have estimated that Chinese rubber demand will rise 5.0 percent in 1997 to 1.47 million tonnes, with domestic output seen at 1.05 million tonnes.
Despite the gap between production and demand, cheaper imports last year sent domestic prices plunging to about 13,000 yuan per tonne, down from a record high of 18,000 yuan the previous two years.
While tappers struggle to raise output, traders on the China-Commodity Futures Exchange in the Hainan capital of Haikou have seen business in latex-based contracts soar.

In 1996, natural rubber was the most heavily traded future on the exchange, with turnover worth 1,273.6 billion yuan -- more than the value of trading in all the exchange's contracts the year before, exchange officials said.
Speculators hungry for risk were behind much of the action, but the exchange's location near the heart of Chinese rubber country made it a natural place to trade on the commodity, they said.
"China is a very big consumer...and also a very big producer," said one exchange manager. "In rubber (futures) everyone looks at Tokyo...but now they are looking at us as well."
